parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Between 4 minutes and 64 minutes, solid ice and liquid water coexist at 0 °C. Compare and contrast the internal energy of an equal mass of solid ice with that of liquid water during this interval.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The liquid water has greater internal energy than the equal mass of ice. Both are at the same temperature, so their molecules have the same average random kinetic energy. The liquid has greater intermolecular potential energy because energy was absorbed during melting to loosen the molecular arrangement.

evidence.detail: May 2024 SL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6711M, PDF page 6, checked against this exact subpart.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A probe is four times as far from the Sun as Earth is. Show that the solar-radiation intensity at the probe is 85 W m⁻². Use the solar constant 1360 W m⁻² at Earth.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

Intensity follows the inverse-square law. Therefore I_probe/I_Earth = (d_Earth/(4d_Earth))² = 1/16, so I_probe = 1360/16 = 85.0 W m⁻².

evidence.detail: May 2024 SL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6711M, PDF page 11, checked against this exact subpart.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Crushed ice of mass 35 g initially at −10 °C warms to 0 °C, as shown on the source graph. The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Show that the average rate at which thermal energy is transferred into the ice is about 3 W.

answer.text: Official markscheme result 3.1 W; editorial worked explanation: The energy needed to warm the ice is Q=mcΔT=(0.035)(2100)(10)=735 J. The graph shows this takes 4.0 min=240 s. Therefore the average transfer rate is P=Q/t=735/240=3.06 W≈3.1 W, which is about 3 W.
answer.evidence: Official May 2024 Physics HL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6708M checked on PDF page(s) 7; editorial explanation independently recalculated against the source task.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Use the 0 °C plateau on the source graph to estimate the specific latent heat of fusion of the 35 g ice sample.

answer.text: Official markscheme result 3.1×10⁵ J kg⁻¹ (3.2×10⁵ J kg⁻¹ also accepted); editorial worked explanation: Reading the graph gives a melting time of about (64−4) min=60 min=3600 s. The transferred energy is Q=Pt=(3.0625)(3600)=1.1025×10⁴ J. Hence L_f=Q/m=(1.1025×10⁴)/0.035=3.15×10⁵ J kg⁻¹≈3.2×10⁵ J kg⁻¹ to two significant figures.

answer.text: Official markscheme conclusion; editorial worked explanation: The equal masses have the same temperature, so their molecules have the same average random kinetic energy. Liquid water has greater internal energy because energy absorbed during fusion increases the intermolecular potential-energy contribution. parts.display_text: A heater supplies 0.12 kW to maintain a capsule surface at 15°C. Its radiating area is 14 m². In this idealized model, neglect incoming thermal radiation and all heat losses except radiation. Estimate the capsule emissivity using σ=5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

answer.text: At constant temperature, heater power balances emitted power: P=εσAT⁴. With P=120 W and T=288.15 K, ε=120/(5.67×10⁻⁸×14×288.15⁴)≈0.0219, about 0.022.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A 0.25 kg block of ice initially at −32°C is placed in water at 0°C in an insulated container. Enough water is present for the final equilibrium temperature to be 0°C. Use cice=2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Lfusion=334000 J kg⁻¹. (a) Calculate the mass of water that freezes. (b) A student says the internal energy of this water is unchanged because it freezes at constant temperature. Explain whether this is correct.

answer.text: (a) Warming the ice needs Q=mcΔT=0.25×2100×32=16800 J. Freezing water releases this energy, so mf=16800/334000=0.0503 kg, about 50 g. (b) The claim is incorrect. Constant temperature means the mean particle kinetic energy is unchanged, but the intermolecular potential energy decreases on freezing. The water releases energy and its internal energy decreases.

A container is wrapped in material of thickness 0.010 m and area 0.060 m². Measurements of outside temperature TG, liquid temperature TL and energy-transfer rate P are:
TG / K: 295, 371, 425, 475, 528
TL / K: 295, 303, 308, 313, 323
P / W: 0.0, 26.3, 43.1, 60.0, 75.0

Choose quantities for a straight-line graph, plot a best-fit line, and use its gradient to determine the thermal conductivity.

answer.text: Plot P vertically against ΔT = TG − TL horizontally. The temperature differences are 0, 68, 117, 162 and 205 K. The gradient is about 0.36 W K⁻¹. From P = kAΔT/L, k = gradient × L/A ≈ 0.060 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: An aluminium block of mass 1.50 kg and specific heat capacity 903 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ absorbs approximately 93 600 J from a particle beam. Its measured temperature rise is 68.0 K. Check whether the measured rise is consistent with this energy input.

answer.text: The measured rise requires Q = mcΔT = 1.50 × 903 × 68.0 = 92 106 J. Alternatively, the input predicts ΔT = 93 600/(1.50 × 903) = 69.1 K. The difference is about 1.6%, so the measured rise is consistent with the approximate input, allowing small energy losses.

A 0.050 kg metal sample at 373 K is placed in 0.100 kg of water at 295 K in an insulated container. They reach 300 K. The water’s specific heat capacity is 4184 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Neglect the container’s heat capacity. What is the metal’s specific heat capacity?

A. 287 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
B. 573 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
C. 2090 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
D. 6620 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

answer.text: B. Energy lost by metal equals energy gained by water: 0.050c(373 − 300) = 0.100 × 4184 × (300 − 295). This gives c ≈ 573 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

A blackbody emits power P₀ with peak wavelength λ₀. Its temperature changes so that the peak wavelength becomes λ₀/2. Its surface area remains constant. What is its new emitted power?

A. P₀/2
B. P₀/16
C. 2P₀
D. 16P₀

answer.text: D. Wien’s law makes the temperature double. Stefan–Boltzmann then gives P/P₀ = (T/T₀)⁴ = 16.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A gas thermometer is placed in thermal contact with a sample. Its large glass bulb and gas must reach the sample’s temperature before a reading is taken.

(a) Explain two limitations caused by this need to reach thermal equilibrium.
(b) Describe one kind of sample or measurement for which this thermometer could still be suitable.

answer.text:
(a) It may respond slowly, so it cannot reliably follow rapidly changing temperatures. It also exchanges energy with the sample while equilibrating, which can significantly change the temperature of a small sample.
(b) It is suitable for a large sample whose temperature remains steady long enough for equilibration, such as a large stable-temperature liquid bath.

parts.display_text: A distant isotropic source has known luminosity L. An observer measures its apparent brightness b, the received power per unit area. Derive an expression for the distance d and state the propagation assumption needed.

answer.text: If radiation spreads uniformly without significant absorption, L is distributed over area 4πd². Thus b = L/(4πd²) and d = √[L/(4πb)]. The method assumes the known luminosity applies and that significant absorption or obscuration is absent or corrected.

A 9.7524 kg aluminium block is heated through 500 K without a change of state. The heat supplied is 4 380 011.1 J. In a repeat under altered conditions, the heat supplied for the same mass and temperature rise is 4 380 022.2 J.

(a) Calculate the specific heat capacity inferred from the first trial, to three significant figures.
(b) Would the repeat give a different value at this precision? Support your answer quantitatively.

answer.text:
(a) c = Q/(mΔT) = 4 380 011.1/(9.7524 × 500) = 898 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ to three significant figures.
(b) The extra 11.1 J changes the inferred c by only 11.1/(9.7524 × 500) = 0.00228 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, about 0.000253%. The repeat therefore also gives 898 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at this precision.

A cylindrical beaker contains liquid with measured height 0.20 m ± 2%, internal diameter 0.05 m ± 3%, and liquid mass 0.36 kg ± 10%. What is the percentage uncertainty in its calculated density?

A. 2%
B. 5%
C. 15%
D. 18%

answer.text: D. ρ = m/(πd²h/4). Percentage uncertainties add with the powers as multipliers: 10% + 2(3%) + 2% = 18%.

parts.display_text:
Metal blocks P and Q are in thermal contact and initially at the same temperature. P has mass 0.54 kg and specific heat capacity 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Q has mass 0.37 kg and specific heat capacity 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A total of 24 kJ is supplied to P, after which the blocks reach a new common temperature. They are insulated from the surroundings.

(a) Define thermal equilibrium.
(b) Find the temperature increase of Q.

answer.text:
(a) The blocks have the same temperature, with no net thermal-energy transfer between them.
(b) They have the same temperature increase ΔT. Energy balance gives 24 000 = [(0.54)(390) + (0.37)(910)]ΔT. Hence ΔT = 43.9 K ≈ 44 K.

answer.text: Because T₂=4T₃ on an absolute temperature scale, sample 2 is hotter. Thermal energy flows spontaneously from sample 2 to sample 3. Net transfer stops when the samples reach the same temperature, that is, thermal equilibrium.

40 cm³ of glycerine of density 1.3 g cm⁻³ is mixed with water of density 1.0 g cm⁻³. Volumes add. What water volume gives mixture density 1.1 g cm⁻³?

A. 4.0 cm³
B. 8.0 cm³
C. 34 cm³
D. 80 cm³

answer.text:
Official key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. Glycerine mass is 1.3×40=52 g. If water volume is V cm³, its mass is V g. Then (52+V)/(40+V)=1.1, so 52+V=44+1.1V and V=80 cm³.
